entry.title: AI2-THOR, ProcTHOR, and Navigation Environment Notes

link.title: AI2-THOR, ProcTHOR, and Navigation Environment Notes

entry.content:
ProcTHOR procedurally generates diverse, interactive indoor environments for embodied-agent research. Sampling virtual homes provides a way to vary layouts and objects rather than train only in a small fixed set of scenes.

The AI2-THOR starting point

My initial installation notes listed:

pip install ai2thor
# Alternative package source recorded in the original note:
conda install -c conda-forge ai2thor

The rest of this notebook was collected while working on a related navigation setup and uses Habitat, HM3D, and UniGoal. Those are separate components: installing Habitat is not itself an installation of ProcTHOR, and the patches below modify UniGoal rather than AI2-THOR.

The adjacent Habitat environment

For that project checkout, I used Python 3.8 with Habitat Sim 0.2.3 and the bundled Habitat Lab dependency:

conda install habitat-sim==0.2.3 -c conda-forge -c aihabitat
pip install -e third_party/habitat-lab

The detailed dependency and debugging notes below overlap with my UniGoal reproduction notebook; I keep the practical steps here because they were part of the original environment record.

Perception and matching dependencies

The navigation stack combined several libraries:

  • LightGlue performs local feature matching with adaptive computation. It can reduce work for easier image pairs and is relevant to reconstruction and localization.
  • Detectron2 provides object detection, instance segmentation, and related vision components. Building it from source can require substantial host memory.
  • Grounded Segment Anything combines SAM’s promptable segmentation with GroundingDINO’s text-guided detection. The pretrained weights make these models useful without training a new detector for every task; “zero-shot” does not mean that the models were never pretrained.
  • Faiss GPU supplies accelerated vector-similarity search and clustering.

I installed the following dependencies from the project root:

pip install git+https://github.com/cvg/LightGlue.git
pip install git+https://github.com/facebookresearch/detectron2.git

git clone https://github.com/IDEA-Research/Grounded-Segment-Anything.git \
  third_party/Grounded-Segment-Anything
cd third_party/Grounded-Segment-Anything
git checkout 5cb813f
pip install -e segment_anything
pip install --no-build-isolation -e GroundingDINO
cd ../../

Checking out that commit places Git in a detached-HEAD state, which is expected when reproducing a particular revision.

Create the destination directory before downloading the model weights. wget -O names the output file; it does not create missing parent directories:

mkdir -p data/models/
wget -O data/models/sam_vit_h_4b8939.pth \
  https://dl.fbaipublicfiles.com/segment_anything/sam_vit_h_4b8939.pth
wget -O data/models/groundingdino_swint_ogc.pth \
  https://github.com/IDEA-Research/GroundingDINO/releases/download/v0.1.0-alpha/groundingdino_swint_ogc.pth

The first file is SAM’s ViT-H checkpoint; the second is GroundingDINO’s Swin-T checkpoint. My transfer logs recorded approximately 2.39 GB and 662 MB respectively.

conda install pytorch::faiss-gpu
pip install -r requirements.txt

When a configured Conda mirror failed, I also recorded an explicit-channel alternative:

conda install faiss-gpu -c pytorch -c nvidia -c anaconda --override-channels

Organize the HM3D data

These steps concern the Habitat/UniGoal evaluation environment. Create the expected locations first:

mkdir -p data/datasets/instance_imagenav/hm3d/v3/
mkdir -p data/scene_datasets/hm3d_v0.2/val/

The source archives in my notes were:

  • HM3D instance-image navigation episodes
  • HM3D v0.2 validation scenes

Obtain the scene data under its applicable access and license terms. From the episode archive, place val, train, and val_mini under data/datasets/instance_imagenav/hm3d/v3/. Place the validation scene directories under data/scene_datasets/hm3d_v0.2/val/.

The file and directory names must match what the configuration expects:

UniGoal/
└── data/
    ├── datasets/
    │   └── instance_imagenav/
    │       └── hm3d/
    │           └── v3/
    │               └── val/
    │                   ├── content/
    │                   │   ├── 4ok3usBNeis.json.gz
    │                   │   ├── 5cdEh9F2hJL.json.gz
    │                   │   └── ...
    │                   └── val.json.gz
    └── scene_datasets/
        └── hm3d_v0.2/
            └── val/
                ├── 00800-TEEsavR23oF/
                │   ├── TEEsavR23oF.basis.glb
                │   └── TEEsavR23oF.basis.navmesh
                ├── 00801-HaxA7YrQdEC/
                └── ...

Configure the language and vision-language models

I used Ollama for this setup. Its Linux installation documentation explains the available installation methods. The command saved in my notebook was:

curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh

On a rented container, I put downloaded models on the data disk:

export OLLAMA_MODELS=/root/autodl-tmp/ollama_models
mkdir -p "$OLLAMA_MODELS"

Set the variable in your own ~/.bashrc if you want it in future interactive shells. If Ollama runs as a system service instead, configure its service environment; changing the current shell does not change an already running service.

Containers without systemd may need a manually started server:

ollama serve &
ollama pull llama3.2-vision

Ollama can resume an interrupted model download. A warning about GPU detection still needs to be checked against the actual machine; it does not establish that GPU inference is working.

Alternatively, use your own model API by configuring llm_model, vlm_model, api_key, and base_url in configs/config_habitat.yaml. Keep an actual API key out of a public configuration file.

Start evaluation

If no Ollama server is running, start one. nohup is an alternative to leaving it attached to the current terminal:

nohup ollama serve > ollama.log 2>&1 &
netstat -tuln | grep 11434
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python main.py

Do not start a second server if port 11434 is already serving the intended instance. This invocation was for the instance-image-goal setup.

On the first run, loading bert-base-uncased failed when Hugging Face was unreachable:

OSError: We couldn't connect to 'https://huggingface.co' to load this file,
couldn't find it in the cached files and it looks like bert-base-uncased
is not the path to a directory containing a file named config.json.

For the network conditions of that run, I tried a mirror before restarting the process:

export HF_ENDPOINT=https://hf-mirror.com

Missing system and Python dependencies

EGL

Importing Habitat Sim failed with:

ImportError: libEGL.so.1: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory

The Ubuntu packages that resolved this in my environment were:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install libegl1 mesa-utils libgl1-mesa-glx

OpenAI client

src/graph/graph.py imported the OpenAI client even in this larger navigation setup:

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'openai'

pip install openai

MKL and Faiss

Importing Faiss then failed because the expected MKL library was missing:

ImportError: libmkl_intel_lp64.so.1: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory

For this older environment, the recorded fix was:

conda install mkl=2021

PyTorch3D

The 3D overlap calculation reached src/graph/utils/iou.py, imported pytorch3d.ops, and failed:

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pytorch3d'

I built PyTorch3D from source in the GPU-enabled environment:

pip install "git+https://github.com/facebookresearch/pytorch3d.git" -v

The build ran from about 23:44 to 00:07 in my notes. That duration is specific to the machine and checkout. Compiler warnings alone did not establish failure; the build’s final status did. My original command appended a machine shutdown, which is not part of installing the package.

NumPy arrays and tensor conversion

At two points in src/graph/graph.py—lines 878 and 903 in the checkout I used—the code called .cpu() on an array that was already a NumPy array:

AttributeError: 'numpy.ndarray' object has no attribute 'cpu'

My immediate workaround was:

frontier_locations = torch.tensor(frontier_locations).cpu().numpy()

A more explicit conversion avoids constructing a tensor unnecessarily:

if isinstance(frontier_locations, torch.Tensor):
    frontier_locations = frontier_locations.detach().cpu().numpy()
else:
    frontier_locations = np.asarray(frontier_locations)

The important point is to know whether each intermediate value is a tensor or an array; the line numbers are only references to that historical checkout.

Keep frontier scores aligned with the same candidates

The next error was a shape mismatch in get_goal, rather than another missing .cpu() method:

scores += distances_16_inverse
ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (1016,) (934,) (1016,)

The two score arrays had been computed over different frontier sets. My patch filtered the candidate positions once, retained those positions as valid_locations, and used exactly that set for both distance terms.

The original pasted function had damaged indentation. The reference below restores the intended block structure and retains the method used in the notebook. It depends on the surrounding project’s imports and class state and has not been validated against newer UniGoal releases.

def get_goal(self, goal=None):
    fbe_map = torch.zeros_like(self.full_map[0, 0])
    if self.full_map.shape[1] == 1:
        fbe_map[self.fbe_free_map[0, 0] > 0] = 1
    else:
        fbe_map[self.full_map[0, 1] > 0] = 1
        obstacles = skimage.morphology.binary_dilation(
            self.full_map[0, 0].cpu().numpy(),
            skimage.morphology.disk(4),
        )
        fbe_map[obstacles] = 3

    fbe_cp = copy.deepcopy(fbe_map)
    fbe_cpp = copy.deepcopy(fbe_map)
    fbe_cp[fbe_cp == 0] = 4  # Unknown space.
    fbe_cp[fbe_cp < 4] = 0   # Free space and obstacles.
    unknown_boundary = skimage.morphology.binary_dilation(
        fbe_cp.cpu().numpy(), skimage.morphology.disk(1)
    )
    fbe_cpp[unknown_boundary] = 0

    frontier_map = (fbe_map - fbe_cpp) == 1
    frontier_map &= (self.num_of_goal < 3).to(frontier_map.device)
    frontier_locations = torch.stack(torch.where(frontier_map), dim=1)
    if frontier_locations.shape[0] == 0:
        return None

    input_pose = np.zeros(7)
    input_pose[:3] = self.full_pose.cpu().numpy()
    input_pose[1] = self.map_size_cm / 100 - input_pose[1]
    input_pose[2] = -input_pose[2]
    input_pose[4] = self.full_map.shape[-2]
    input_pose[6] = self.full_map.shape[-1]
    traversible, start = self.get_traversible(
        self.full_map.cpu().numpy()[0, 0, ::-1], input_pose
    )

    planner = FMMPlanner(traversible)
    planner.set_goal([start[0] + 1, start[1] + 1])
    fmm_dist = planner.fmm_dist[::-1]

    # Convert once and account for the planner's coordinate offset.
    frontier_locations_np = frontier_locations.cpu().numpy() + 1
    distances = fmm_dist[
        frontier_locations_np[:, 0], frontier_locations_np[:, 1]
    ] / 20

    distance_threshold = 3
    valid_mask = distances >= distance_threshold
    valid_distances = distances[valid_mask]
    valid_locations = frontier_locations_np[valid_mask]
    if len(valid_distances) == 0:
        return None

    scores = 10 - (
        np.clip(valid_distances, 0, 10 + distance_threshold)
        - distance_threshold
    )

    if isinstance(goal, (list, np.ndarray)):
        try:
            planner_goal = FMMPlanner(traversible)
            planner_goal.set_goal([int(goal[0]) + 1, int(goal[1]) + 1])
            fmm_dist_goal = planner_goal.fmm_dist[::-1]

            # Use the same filtered candidates as the first score term.
            goal_distances = fmm_dist_goal[
                valid_locations[:, 0], valid_locations[:, 1]
            ] / 20
            goal_scores = 1 - (
                np.clip(goal_distances, 0, 10 + distance_threshold)
                - distance_threshold
            ) / 10
            scores += goal_scores
        except Exception as error:
            print(f"Goal processing error: {error}")

    if len(scores) == 0:
        return None
    best_idx = np.argmax(scores)
    return valid_locations[best_idx] - 1

The coordinate offsets, distance scaling by 20, and threshold 3 are parameters from that implementation, not universal navigation defaults.

An unrecognized goal category

Later, set_goal_cat_id attempted to look up a category that was absent from the environment’s category map:

self.info['goal_name'] = self.index2name[idx]
KeyError: 6

In src/agent/unigoal/agent.py, my patch checked the proposed category before returning it. The surrounding center-of-image test was retained:

image_height, image_width = self.instance_imagegoal.shape[:2]
box = ins_whwh[0][2]
center_dx = (box[0] + box[2] - image_width) / 2
center_dy = (box[1] + box[3] - image_height) / 2

if center_dx**2 + center_dy**2 < 2 * (image_width / 6)**2:
    cat_id = int(ins_whwh[0][0])
    if cat_id in self.envs.index2name:
        return cat_id
return None

This prevents that invalid category from reaching the dictionary lookup. It does not establish that the detector’s category mapping is semantically correct; that mapping still needs to agree with the environment.

The notebook ended with a plan to add episode selection in main.py, but no implementation was recorded.
entry.summary: An introduction to procedural indoor environments, followed by the Habitat and UniGoal setup notes collected alongside them.

entry.title: Reproducing UniGoal on a GPU Server

link.title: Reproducing UniGoal on a GPU Server

entry.content:
This notebook documents my attempt to reproduce UniGoal, a universal zero-shot goal-navigation framework. UniGoal is the work being reproduced here; the method and benchmark results in the introduction are not my own contributions.

What the method does

UniGoal represents both the observed environment and the requested goal as graphs, allowing object categories, target images, and text descriptions to share a navigation pipeline. RGB-D observations update the scene graph, while language and vision-language models help form the goal representation.

The exploration policy changes with the degree of graph matching. With no useful match, it explores using decomposed subgraphs; with a partial match, it projects coordinates and aligns anchors to infer a promising target location; with a full match, it checks and refines the localization. A record of unsuccessful regions reduces repeated visits.

The overview I read described comparisons on Matterport3D and HM3D against methods including Mod-IIN, SG-Nav, and GOAT. It quoted success rates of 41.0% for object navigation, 60.2% for instance-image navigation, and 20.2% for text navigation. Those figures are reported context from that overview, not results reproduced by the installation steps below; comparisons require the original paper’s exact task and evaluation settings.

Create the environment

The rented base image advertised PyTorch 2.5.1, Python 3.12, Ubuntu 22.04, and CUDA 12.4. The older Habitat stack required a separate Python 3.8 environment:

git clone https://github.com/bagh2178/UniGoal.git
cd UniGoal
conda create -n unigoal python=3.8
conda activate unigoal

On the AutoDL image, I used its network helper when available and removed stale proxy variables from the shell:

source /etc/network_turbo
unset http_proxy https_proxy

That helper is platform-specific; it is not a standard Linux configuration file.

Install Habitat Sim and Habitat Lab

conda install habitat-sim==0.2.3 withbullet headless \
  -c conda-forge -c aihabitat --override-channels
pip install -e third_party/habitat-lab

An unrecognized goal category

Later, set_goal_cat_id attempted to look up a category that was absent from the environment’s category map:

self.info['goal_name'] = self.index2name[idx]
KeyError: 6

In src/agent/unigoal/agent.py, my patch checked the proposed category before returning it. The surrounding center-of-image test was retained:

image_height, image_width = self.instance_imagegoal.shape[:2]
box = ins_whwh[0][2]
center_dx = (box[0] + box[2] - image_width) / 2
center_dy = (box[1] + box[3] - image_height) / 2

if center_dx**2 + center_dy**2 < 2 * (image_width / 6)**2:
    cat_id = int(ins_whwh[0][0])
    if cat_id in self.envs.index2name:
        return cat_id
return None

This prevents that invalid category from reaching the dictionary lookup. It does not establish that the detector’s category mapping is semantically correct; that mapping still needs to agree with the environment.

The notebook ended with a plan to add episode selection in main.py, but no implementation was recorded.
entry.summary: Habitat setup, model downloads, HM3D data organization, and the frontier-planning errors I encountered while reproducing UniGoal.

entry.title: AutoDL Notes: Moving Instances and Fine-Tuning OpenVLA

link.title: AutoDL Notes: Moving Instances and Fine-Tuning OpenVLA

entry.content:
For my experiments, I tried both AutoDL and GPUShare. GPUShare offered a student-verification process worth checking at the time. The AutoDL documentation was my main reference for instance management.

Restarting and cloning an instance

I found that restarting an existing instance depended on GPU availability on its original host, rather than free GPUs elsewhere in the region. That made it easy to have an intact environment but no immediately available GPU on that particular machine.

The cloning feature let me copy the system and data disks to another instance in the same region. My notes recorded a limit of three clones per day at the time; that is a historical observation, not a statement of the platform’s current quota.

Copying data between instances

Cross-instance copying was another way to move a prepared environment or experiment data to an available instance without starting the setup from scratch.

My original notebook also contained Docker commands copied from an unrelated setup. The relevant Docker troubleshooting is now kept in the DreamWaQ and Docker note.

Match the OpenVLA command to the checkout

The more useful lesson from this notebook was that similarly named fine-tuning scripts can expose different command-line options. A command using --use_l1_regression, --use_diffusion, or --use_proprio does not necessarily work with the original OpenVLA fine-tuning script.

I recorded the following extended-interface run for a LIBERO goal dataset:

torchrun --standalone --nnodes 1 --nproc-per-node 1 vla-scripts/finetune.py \
  --vla_path openvla/openvla-7b \
  --data_root_dir /root/autodl-tmp/openvla/dataset/ \
  --dataset_name libero_goal_no_noops \
  --run_root_dir /root/autodl-tmp/openvla/log/ \
  --use_l1_regression True \
  --use_diffusion False \
  --use_film False \
  --num_images_in_input 2 \
  --use_proprio True \
  --batch_size 8 \
  --learning_rate 5e-4 \
  --num_steps_before_decay 100000 \
  --max_steps 150005 \
  --save_freq 10000 \
  --save_latest_checkpoint_only False \
  --image_aug True \
  --lora_rank 32 \
  --wandb_entity YOUR_WANDB_ENTITY \
  --wandb_project YOUR_WANDB_PROJECT

However, the help output from a different checkout listed --save_steps, --grad_accumulation_steps, --adapter_tmp_dir, --use_lora, and --use_quantization, without those extended action-head options. I adjusted the command to that interface:

torchrun --standalone --nnodes 1 --nproc-per-node 1 vla-scripts/finetune.py \
  --vla_path /root/autodl-tmp/openvla/openvla-7b \
  --data_root_dir /root/autodl-tmp/openvla/dataset/modified_libero_rlds/ \
  --dataset_name libero_object_no_noops \
  --run_root_dir /root/autodl-tmp/openvla/log/ \
  --adapter_tmp_dir /root/autodl-tmp/openvla/log/ \
  --lora_rank 32 \
  --batch_size 2 \
  --grad_accumulation_steps 1 \
  --learning_rate 2.5e-4 \
  --image_aug True \
  --wandb_project YOUR_WANDB_PROJECT \
  --wandb_entity YOUR_WANDB_ENTITY \
  --save_steps 5000 \
  --max_steps 30000 \
  --save_latest_checkpoint_only true

For the extended interface, I also saved a smaller-batch variant using local model weights:

torchrun --standalone --nnodes 1 --nproc-per-node 1 vla-scripts/finetune.py \
  --vla_path ./weight/openvla-7b \
  --data_root_dir ../modified_libero_rlds/ \
  --dataset_name libero_goal_no_noops \
  --run_root_dir ./log \
  --use_l1_regression True \
  --use_diffusion False \
  --use_film False \
  --num_images_in_input 2 \
  --use_proprio True \
  --batch_size 4 \
  --learning_rate 5e-4 \
  --num_steps_before_decay 100000 \
  --max_steps 150005 \
  --save_freq 10000 \
  --save_latest_checkpoint_only True \
  --image_aug True \
  --lora_rank 32

The /root/autodl-tmp paths reflect the rented container’s storage layout. Replace them with the paths for the actual instance, and inspect python vla-scripts/finetune.py --help before choosing among these examples. These notes record launch configurations, not a completed evaluation of the trained policies.
entry.summary: Practical notes from using rented GPUs, copying environments, and matching OpenVLA commands to the repository version.

entry.title: Keeping Training Sessions Alive with tmux

link.title: Keeping Training Sessions Alive with tmux

entry.content:
Losing a training run halfway through because an SSH connection dropped was enough motivation to learn tmux.

Separate the session from the terminal

A process launched directly from an SSH shell can receive a hangup when the connection closes. Whether it survives depends on how it was started and how it handles that signal. tmux provides a persistent terminal session on the server that you can detach from and reconnect to later.

It also supports multiple windows and split panes inside a session. More than one client can attach to the same session when shared access is appropriate.

The essential commands

Create a named session:

tmux new -s training

Start the training command inside it. To detach, press Ctrl+b, release both keys, then press d. You can also run:

tmux detach

After reconnecting over SSH, list the sessions and attach:

tmux list-sessions
tmux attach -t training

A session can also be addressed by its numeric ID:

tmux attach -t 0

Rename a session or deliberately end one:

tmux rename-session -t 0 new-name
tmux kill-session -t training

Killing the session ends the terminal context containing the jobs, so it is different from detaching.

My minimal workflow

# On the server:
tmux new -s my_session
# Run the training command, then press Ctrl+b followed by d.

# After a later SSH login:
tmux attach-session -t my_session

When there is only one session, tmux attach is enough. The session survives a client disconnect; it does not survive a server shutdown or guarantee that the training program itself will not fail.
entry.summary: A short guide to creating, detaching, and recovering terminal sessions after an SSH disconnect.

entry.title: Working Considerately on a Shared GPU Server

link.title: Working Considerately on a Shared GPU Server

entry.content:
A labmate arranged access to an Ubuntu server and gave me a user account. My first question was how to run experiments without disrupting everyone else’s environment or jobs. These are the practices and small scripts I collected while using the shared A800 machine.

Start with your own shell configuration

A minimal $ prompt can simply mean the account is using a minimal shell configuration. To work in Bash:

bash

Keep environment changes in your own ~/.profile or ~/.bashrc. Editing /etc/profile, /etc/bashrc, or another global configuration can affect every user. Installing Conda in your own home directory is different from replacing system CUDA libraries or a GPU driver.

Select an existing CUDA toolkit

I used the toolkit installations already maintained under /usr/local. The helper below lists them when sourced without an argument and selects one for the current shell when given a version:

source switch-cuda.sh
source switch-cuda.sh 12.4

For example, the machine had cuda-11.0 and cuda-12.4. Save this as switch-cuda.sh:

#!/usr/bin/env bash

# Source this file so the environment changes affect the current shell.
if [[ "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}" == "${0}" ]]; then
    echo "Please use 'source switch-cuda.sh [VERSION]'."
    exit 1
fi

cuda_install_folder="/usr/local"
cuda_target_version="${1:-}"

if [[ -z "$cuda_target_version" ]]; then
    echo "CUDA installations in ${cuda_install_folder}:"
    for cuda_candidate in "$cuda_install_folder"/cuda-[0-9]*; do
        [[ -d "$cuda_candidate" ]] && echo "* ${cuda_candidate##*/}"
    done
    return 0
fi

cuda_selected_path="$cuda_install_folder/cuda-$cuda_target_version"
if [[ ! -d "$cuda_selected_path" ]]; then
    echo "CUDA ${cuda_target_version} was not found."
    return 1
fi

# Remove old toolkit paths while retaining other entries.
IFS=: read -r -a cuda_path_entries <<< "$PATH"
cuda_new_path="$cuda_selected_path/bin"
for cuda_entry in "${cuda_path_entries[@]}"; do
    [[ "$cuda_entry" == "$cuda_install_folder"/cuda* ]] && continue
    cuda_new_path+=":$cuda_entry"
done

IFS=: read -r -a cuda_library_entries <<< "${LD_LIBRARY_PATH:-}"
cuda_new_library_path="$cuda_selected_path/lib64:$cuda_selected_path/extras/CUPTI/lib64"
for cuda_entry in "${cuda_library_entries[@]}"; do
    [[ -z "$cuda_entry" || "$cuda_entry" == "$cuda_install_folder"/cuda* ]] && continue
    cuda_new_library_path+=":$cuda_entry"
done

export CUDA_HOME="$cuda_selected_path"
export CUDA_ROOT="$cuda_selected_path"
export PATH="$cuda_new_path"
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="$cuda_new_library_path"
echo "Switched to CUDA ${cuda_target_version}."

This selects a toolkit for the shell; it does not change the system driver or guarantee that a particular PyTorch build uses that toolkit. The script is a cleaned-up version of the helper in my original note, without changing the shell’s global errexit setting.

Install Conda for your account

I preferred Miniconda for its smaller initial footprint:

mkdir -p ~/miniconda-installer
cd ~/miniconda-installer
wget https://repo.anaconda.com/miniconda/Miniconda3-latest-Linux-x86_64.sh
bash Miniconda3-latest-Linux-x86_64.sh

After installing to the default location:

eval "$("$HOME/miniconda3/bin/conda" shell.bash hook)"
conda init bash

The installer and conda init can update your own shell configuration. Choose package channels within that environment as needed. System packages installed through APT still normally require administrator access; selecting a different mirror does not remove that requirement.

Find out who is using a GPU

A continuously refreshed status view is useful before starting a job:

watch -n 2 -d nvidia-smi

Given a process ID from the output, inspect its owner and start time:

ps -p PID -o user=,lstart=

I also used a small script to put process ownership beside the GPU index. Save it as check.sh, then run bash check.sh:

#!/usr/bin/env bash

pids=$(nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=pid --format=csv,noheader | sort -u)
if [[ -z "$pids" ]]; then
    echo "No compute processes are running on the GPU."
    exit 0
fi

printf "%-10s %-20s %-25s %s\n" "PID" "USER" "STARTED" "GPU"
while IFS= read -r pid; do
    process_user=$(ps -p "$pid" -o user=)
    process_started=$(ps -p "$pid" -o lstart=)
    gpu_index=$(nvidia-smi pmon -c 1 | awk -v pid="$pid" '$2 == pid {print $1}')
    printf "%-10s %-20s %-25s %s\n" \
      "$pid" "$process_user" "$process_started" "$gpu_index"
done <<< "$pids"

A process can exit between queries, and visibility depends on the server configuration. The point is to identify the owner and coordinate GPU usage, rather than terminate someone else’s training job.

A small Vim reminder

For local configuration edits:

vim ~/.bashrc

Use i to edit, Esc to leave insert mode, and :wq to save and quit.
entry.summary: Personal environments, CUDA selection, and process inspection on a shared Ubuntu A800 server.

entry.title: Installing Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab on a Server

link.title: Installing Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab on a Server

entry.content:
This note records an Isaac Sim 4.2 installation from December 2024. The commands refer to the repository layouts and package versions used then; newer Isaac Lab releases may organize their tutorials differently.

I started with a Python environment containing PyTorch and CUDA support. One version recorded in my notes was:

pip install torch==2.4.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu118

For the complete setup requirements, see the Isaac Lab pip installation guide.

Install Isaac Sim

The full version-pinned installation was:

pip install --upgrade pip
pip install \
  isaacsim==4.2.0.2 \
  isaacsim-extscache-physics==4.2.0.2 \
  isaacsim-extscache-kit==4.2.0.2 \
  isaacsim-extscache-kit-sdk==4.2.0.2 \
  --extra-index-url https://pypi.nvidia.com

I also recorded a component-based alternative for the functionality I needed:

pip install isaacsim-rl isaacsim-replicator isaacsim-extscache-physics \
  isaacsim-extscache-kit-sdk isaacsim-extscache-kit isaacsim-app \
  --extra-index-url https://pypi.nvidia.com

That alternative is unpinned, so it is not an exact recreation of the versioned environment above. Check that the selected component versions are compatible before combining them.

Launch the application to check startup:

isaacsim
# When intentionally running as root in a container:
isaacsim --allow-root

The first launch asks for acceptance of NVIDIA’s license agreement. It can then spend considerable time resolving and downloading extensions. My log progressed from:

Failed to solve some dependencies locally, syncing with extension registry...

to:

[7042.715s] [ext: omni.app.mini-0.1.1] startup
[7042.733s] app ready

The initial startup took much longer than I expected; the final app ready line was the useful signal.

Clone and install Isaac Lab

Public repositories can be cloned over HTTPS without configuring an SSH key:

git clone https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacLab.git
sudo apt install cmake build-essential
cd IsaacLab

An SSH clone instead uses a key registered with your own GitHub account. My original note confused this with adding a key to someone else’s repository.

If the helper script is not executable, give that file execute permission:

chmod +x isaaclab.sh

Install all supported learning frameworks, or select one:

./isaaclab.sh --install
# Alternative: install only rl_games.
./isaaclab.sh --install rl_games

Other choices in the version I used included rsl_rl, sb3, skrl, robomimic, and none.

I verified the installation with the empty-scene tutorial:

./isaaclab.sh -p source/standalone/tutorials/00_sim/create_empty.py
# Or, from the configured virtual environment:
python source/standalone/tutorials/00_sim/create_empty.py

Robot Lab examples

I then followed Robot Lab, cloning it separately from the Isaac Lab checkout:

cd ..
git clone https://github.com/fan-ziqi/robot_lab.git
cd robot_lab
python -m pip install -e ./exts/robot_lab
python scripts/tools/list_envs.py

The interpreter used for the editable installation must be the one configured for Isaac Lab. The following commands are examples saved from that setup:

python scripts/rsl_rl/base/train.py \
  --task RobotLab-Isaac-Velocity-Flat-Unitree-G1-v0 \
  --headless --video --video_length 100 --video_interval 500 \
  --num_envs 32 --max_iterations 10000

python3 scripts/rsl_rl/train.py \
  --task Template-Isaac-Reach-UR10-v0 \
  --num_envs 4096 --headless --video --video_length 100 \
  --max_iterations 10

The first is a Unitree G1 locomotion task; the second is a UR10 reaching task. Their task names and entry points depend on the corresponding extension version.
entry.summary: My December 2024 setup notes for Isaac Sim 4.2, Isaac Lab, and robot training examples.

entry.title: A Remote Ubuntu Desktop with Xfce and VNC

link.title: A Remote Ubuntu Desktop with Xfce and VNC

entry.content:
Some simulator debugging is easier with a desktop. These notes describe the Xfce and TightVNC setup I used on a FunHPC container, based on the platform’s VNC guide.

Install the desktop packages

These are Ubuntu packages installed with APT, rather than Python packages:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install xorg openbox xfce4 xfce4-goodies tightvncserver

The original container ran as root. If a minimal container has not set USER, initialize it for the actual account:

export USER="$(id -un)"

Configure the VNC session

Start VNC once and set its password when prompted:

vncserver

Then stop that first display before changing its startup file:

vncserver -kill :1
vim ~/.vnc/xstartup

In Vim, press i to edit, Esc to leave insert mode, and :wq to save. The relevant Xfce startup commands are:

xrdb "$HOME/.Xresources"
startxfce4 &

Make the file executable, then launch the desktop at the desired size:

chmod +x ~/.vnc/xstartup
vncserver -localhost -geometry 1280x960

The first display is usually :1, corresponding to port 5901.

Create the tunnel from the local computer

Run the following on your own computer, replacing the placeholders with the SSH connection details provided by the platform:

ssh -p SSH_PORT -N -L 5901:localhost:5901 USER@SERVER_HOST

The command remains in the foreground and may print nothing after authentication. That is normal: it is maintaining the forwarding connection. On first connection, check the server’s host-key fingerprint against the platform’s information before accepting it.

My original post included a temporary cloud hostname, port, and connection transcript. Those were specific to that instance; the parameterized command above is the reusable part.

Connect the VNC viewer

Install a client such as RealVNC Viewer, connect to:

localhost:5901

and enter the VNC password configured earlier. Keep the SSH tunnel open for the duration of the desktop session.
entry.summary: Setting up a graphical desktop on a FunHPC server and reaching it through an SSH tunnel.

entry.title: Finding an Entry Point for a Literature Survey

link.title: Finding an Entry Point for a Literature Survey

entry.content:
This was the beginning of my literature-search workflow in November 2024. I was trying to investigate quadruped robotics and needed a concrete first step before attempting a full survey.

Start with the terminology

Before searching for papers, I collected the English terms used to describe the topic. ChatGPT, Tencent Yuanbao, and Youdao helped me move between Chinese descriptions and English search phrases.

My initial keyword list was:

quadrupedal
robots
quadruped

Combining them into a phrase such as quadrupedal robots gave me an entry point in Google Scholar. From there, I could open a promising paper and inspect the terms its authors used.

Keep the scope honest

The original notebook stopped after this first search step. It did not yet contain a completed review, a systematic screening protocol, or results from using AI to synthesize the papers. I keep it here as a small record of how I started, alongside the more developed prompt examples.
entry.summary: A short research notebook on turning an unfamiliar topic into searchable terms, using quadruped robotics as an example.

entry.title: Prompt Patterns for Literature Search and Review

link.title: Prompt Patterns for Literature Search and Review

entry.content:
I initially had little patience for elaborate prompt templates. These examples grew out of experiments with GPT-4o in November 2024, when I found that a clear scope and an explicit output format made literature work easier to inspect.

A Markdown reference was useful when preparing the inputs and outputs.

A basic structure

The labels below are prompts for thinking, rather than fields that every request needs:

Role:
Task:
Instructions:
Required steps:
Requirements:
Context:
Examples or input:
Output format:

Finding representative papers

This example comes from work on multimodal discourse analysis in translation studies:

Role:
You are a researcher familiar with multimodal translation studies and
its theoretical development.

Task:
Use web search to identify five representative academic publications
on applications of multimodal discourse analysis in translation studies.

Requirements:
- Use established scholarly databases, publisher websites, or journals.
- Select peer-reviewed journal articles or conference papers.
- Do not invent references. If a bibliographic detail cannot be verified,
  state what is missing.
- Consider influential work, authors with substantive contributions,
  and papers that illustrate important theoretical or recent developments.
- Treat citation counts as one signal, not proof of methodological quality.

Output:
For each paper, provide its title, authors, year, a short summary,
and a source link that allows me to verify the publication.

I repeated the search with different keywords and perspectives to expand the reading list. Repeating the same request alone does not guarantee new or representative references; I still checked the sources.

Summarizing and synthesizing a supplied reading set

The second prompt deliberately limits the evidence to nine attached papers:

Task:
Summarize and analyze the nine attached papers, then write a focused
literature review on multimodal discourse analysis and translation studies.

Step 1: Summarize and organize the papers.
- Give a concise account of each paper's central question and contribution.
- Group the nine papers into no more than three thematic categories.
- Avoid categories that substantially overlap.
- Identify the authors and year of each paper in every category.

Step 2: Write the review.
- Explain the main research directions and the substance of each category.
- Discuss how multimodal discourse analysis has been applied to translation.
- Identify limitations or open questions supported by this reading set.

Scope:
Use only the contents of the attached papers. Do not expand the review
with unsupported claims about the wider field. Focus on the international
research discussed in these papers and its applications to translation.

Suggested structure:
Paragraph 1: Introduce the thematic categories, explain their main concerns,
and connect representative author-year examples to translation applications.
Paragraph 2: Discuss the limitations and gaps that follow from the evidence.

The useful distinction was between collecting sources and making claims from sources. The search prompt produces a reading list; the synthesis prompt works from the papers themselves.
entry.summary: An experimental notebook of prompts I used with GPT-4o to find, organize, and discuss academic literature.

entry.title: Installing Docker on an Ubuntu GPU Server

link.title: Installing Docker on an Ubuntu GPU Server

entry.content:
This is the Docker installation sequence I recorded on an Ubuntu GPU server in November 2024. Although the original note’s title mentioned having no sudo access, the system-package and service commands below require an administrator or a root shell. They are not a rootless Docker installation procedure.

Remove conflicting packages

On a machine being prepared for this installation, I first removed the older Docker packages:

sudo apt-get remove docker docker-engine docker.io containerd runc

Package names vary by Ubuntu release; these are the names in the original setup.

Add the repository

Install the tools needed for HTTPS repositories and key handling:

sudo apt install apt-transport-https ca-certificates curl \
  software-properties-common gnupg lsb-release

Choose one repository source. For Docker’s official repository:

curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg \
  | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/docker-archive-keyring.gpg

echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/docker-archive-keyring.gpg] https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu $(lsb_release -cs) stable" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list > /dev/null

When access to the official host was unreliable, I used the Aliyun mirror instead:

curl -fsSL https://mirrors.aliyun.com/docker-ce/linux/ubuntu/gpg \
  | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/docker-archive-keyring.gpg

echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/docker-archive-keyring.gpg] https://mirrors.aliyun.com/docker-ce/linux/ubuntu $(lsb_release -cs) stable" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list > /dev/null

Both examples write the same source file; use the one appropriate to the installation, then refresh the package index:

sudo apt update

Install and inspect Docker

sudo apt install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io
docker version
sudo systemctl start docker
systemctl status docker

Starting Docker does not by itself configure NVIDIA GPU support; this note covers the base Docker installation.

Shell completion

I installed Bash completion and loaded Docker’s completion script:

sudo apt-get install bash-completion
sudo curl -L \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/docker/docker-ce/master/components/cli/contrib/completion/bash/docker \
  -o /etc/bash_completion.d/docker.sh
source /etc/bash_completion.d/docker.sh

That script URL belongs to the repository layout used in the original note. If it has moved, use the completion support supplied by the installed Docker package.
entry.summary: The package, repository, service, and shell-completion steps from my Ubuntu Docker setup.
